newsitem.title: GREECE: GREEK '97 FOREX POLICY STABLE AND INFLATION-MINDED.
newsitem.headline: GREEK '97 FOREX POLICY STABLE AND INFLATION-MINDED.

text.p: ATHENS, Jan 31 - Bank of Greece will pursue a stable but more flexible foreign exchange policy in 1997 in a bid to curb inflation to 4.5 percent by end-97 and below 3.0 percent by end-98, its governor Lucas Papademos said on Friday.

"The policy for the foreign exchange rate of the drachma is defined by the top priority of curbing inflation," said Papademos. "Specifically, the stability of the foreign exchange rate of the drachma against the currencies that make up the ecu will be the main goal of monetary policy."
The drachma slid by 1.0 percent against the ecu in 1996 and 3.0 percent in 1995.

The so-called hard drachma policy, which limits the sliding of the dollar against the ecu and other EMS currencies by less than inflation differentials justify, has been instrumental in reducing inflation.
Bank of Greece figures showed that imported wholesale price inflation was in negative territory, registering a drop of 0.6 percent year-on-year in November 1996.

The credibility of the central bank's hard drachma policy and interest rate differentials favouring the drachma have attracted huge capital inflows, beefing up the country's foreign exchange reserves and boosting interbank liquidity.

The central bank has been sterilising foreign exchange inflows by draining excess interbank liquidity to prevent it from spilling over to the rest of the economy, threatening its intermediate monetary goals and fuelling inflation.
Limited progress in addressing fiscal imbalances has forced the monetary and forex policy to bear the burden of the fight against inflation.

"The direction of foreign exchange policy will remain definitely anti-inflationary but its execution will be characterised by greater flexibility than in the past, taking into consideration the inflationary pressures as well as the prevailing conditions in money and forex markets," he said.
Asked when the drachma will join the ERM, Papademos said it was still early to set an ERM entry date.
"It is premature," he said. "Anyway, we will have a new ERM at the begining of 1999."
The ERM entry date was linked to developments in inflation and other economic indicators, said Papademos.
The drachma is not part of the current ERM but government officials have said it will join the mechanism as soon as economic conditions allowed it.
Greece hopes to be in the second wave of EU countries joining the EMU. Countries aspiring to enter the EMU should have their currencies spend at least two years in the currency grid.
Asked if a rising dollar would alter Greece's forex policy, Papademos said it could happen if excessive dollar swings threatened the country's inflation goal.
He said $/drachma rate traced to a great extend the price of the dollar against other major currencies in international markets.
